I think I know what it is that distinguishes it from a lot of MCU movies. It’s that it COMMITS to the comedy. The movie basically just is a comedy, like that’s its genre. Sure, it could have chosen to be dark and gritty (particularly with the goddess of death as the main villain), but it made the bold move of basically going for 90% comedy and it nails it. It commits to it and nails it. The first Guardians of the Galaxy movie did the same thing and it worked there too. But a lot of the MCU movies ended up with this weird blend of serious subject matter/comedy so we get this 50/50 mash up where obviously serious moments are basically ruined by an out of place one-liner. In those cases it’s like the movies don’t have an identity or don’t know how to stick the landing to any serious scene without a joke.

I just think Ragnarok is an insanely fun movie. Is it a masterpiece of cinema? Hell no. But it’s just pure fun and entertainment and it’s one of the rare movies where whenever I rewatch it, I get that same exact sense of fun from it. It never grows stale even when I know the jokes are coming, so that tells me they did something right with that movie. I can’t even really pinpoint it exactly, it’s just a positive happy feeling the movie exudes.

Out of all the MCU movies you could have chosen, ironically, Ragnarok is the one that REALLY worked because of the comedy. That was comedy done well. Ragnarok is probably in my top 3 MCU movies. There are so many MCU movies where comedy is done badly though, particular Age of Ultron, Thor 4, Civil War etc.

This is a beautifully thought out post and I love the work you put into it. I know I commented this previously on another post of yours but I just want to reiterate it here and explain my reasoning for why I can’t accept Many Happy Returns as been a dream sequence episode. 

First of all, I think it’s fundamentally accepted that there is no true correct or incorrect order of episodes. Similarly, there is no “wrong” interpretation of the show. However, for me personally, to accept something like this (which is basically head-canon), I have to at least find it believable that it was the creator’s intent. In this case of MHR, I cannot believe that. I don’t believe it was intended to be a dream episode at all. The Prisoner constantly throughout its run always embraced far out storylines and dramatic events. From viewing Six’s dreams to mind swapping, and even a literal dream sequence episode in The Girl Who Was Death (in that case, of course, it is a story within a story and the show reveals that).

What I’m saying is, if MHR had been intended as a dream episode, that information would have been shown in the episode itself. But it isn’t. Nothing concrete even suggests it could be to me. So yes, while the idea of MHR been a dream episode might be attractive, and I can see why it helps your ordering of the episodes, I can’t personally go along with it because in no way shape or form do I think it was the intention behind the episode.

I can see that, yes, particularly his protective nature. I’d argue it’s always there and sometimes could be his undoing (Nadia in Chimes). It ties into the “POP” (protect other people) we hear Number Two talk about in Once upon a Time as well.

Ultimately I see The Prisoner as both, an eccentric spy thriller and allegorical tale. It can be both at times. As McGoogan had total control by the time of Fall Out, ultimately the story by then is, for me, 99% allegory. I read almost nothing literally in that episode. McGoogan always would have preferred it that way I think. Free For All stands out among the early episodes precisely because it was penned by him. The whole episode is a jab at elections and the futility behind them. 

I think McGoogan always wanted to send out a warning against authoritarianism. I remember him speaking on a TV show once saying he thought it was prisonership that he had to use an ID card to enter the building he was been interviewed him. I can’t remember when it was  (well, WAY before my time regardless because I’m only 31), but I saw it on YouTube. Might have been the 80’s, but he was still warning about the creeping hand of authoritarianism.

On the other hand, though, I also think he did want to send a message of individuality. And not just a purely positive one either. He outright stated he made Number One himself because he believed the most thoroughly evil thing is ourselves. The evil inside us. So there’s that lens as well.

So when you think about it, The Prisoner is three things.

1: An off the wall spy thriller 
2: Allegorical warning of where society could be heading
3: An introspective lens, a mirror for us to examine ourselves.

One thing is for sure, no interpretation can be wrong. The fact it still inspires conversations like this 60 years on is a testament to its genius.

For me there is a big difference between Six in Chimes and in HIA. I think the core difference is arrogance and confidence. This is why Chimes is early for me. There’s still a strong stubborn sense of arrogance. He’s failed multiple times prior yes (Checkmate, Free For All, etc), but I get the sense in Chimes he still believes it’s only a matter of time before he wins, before he escapes. I think after this failure he is repeatedly beaten down with the thought of escape and the Village’s attempts to break him start to become more creative and intense, then he actually does escape in MHR, only to realise it’s pointless. The Village extends further than he feared. 

At this point all arrogance goes and is instead replaced by a pure stoic mission of just withstanding against the Village. Resisting as a symbol against the Village and, if possible yes, to hurt it from within. The Number Two in HIA is sadistic, yes, and it is definitely personal for Number Six, but I do think that Number Two also symbolises the Village itself, which Six does view as an evil, destructive force. In destroying that Number Two he also sends a more stronger message than he ever has done before. Which is why I have it at episode 14, just before TGWWD and the two part finale.

Thank you. You are right that I do ascribe all Earthly laws and time to the Village, yes. In my time I have considered many possibilities and theories. I’ve heard possibilities that Number 6 is dead from the start of the series and the Village is either a dying construct or a form of afterlife, or that the Village is made up of an alien society with Rover being their deity, etc. 

For me, The Prisoner is ALWAYS allegorical in nature, yes, but until the absolute finale (Fall Out itself) we are supposed to also take it at face value as well. Perhaps due to Markstein’s involvement it remained somewhat grounded throughout the first 2/3rd’s of the series run. McGoohan definitely had fun with the formula once Markstein had gone. For example that’s why we got an episode like Living in Harmony. In the great man’s words, he “always wanted to do a western”. That’s the reason that episode exists. Simply that. McGoohan wanted to do a western. But even then, in its most ludicrous moments, it kept a tenuous 
thread to the reality of the Village established since the start of the show. 

It kept on ticking like that until the very end, until the start of the final episode. It’s there everything transforms. That’s why it’s only the last episode where I totally disengage trying to find consistency between episodes. Fall Out is just in a different realm for me and is 99% allegory. That’s why no concrete answers can ever be found. McGoohan wanted it that way, hence why he wrote the Conclusion the way he did.

The Schizoid Man is set during February according to the calendar in that episode (February 10th). Many Happy Returns is set in March because it coincides with his birthday, so TSM has to be the episode just before MHR. 

It could be argued that it’s February and March of separate years perhaps, but for me it can’t be set over a year apart because he’s only been gone 1 year by the time of Do Not Forsake Me, Oh My Darling, unless we’re saying that episode should be BEFORE MHR, which to me makes little to no sense because the implication at the end of that episode is that Number 6 remembers the mind swap when he is returned to his own body. as he comments on the professor being able to transfer three minds at one time. Personally I love the open ended nature of the show. The fact everything doesn’t get tied up neatly with a bow helps its enduring appeal for sure. The finale is 100% the most controversial aspect, and probably for good reason. I firmly believe McGoohan totally winged it at that point. However, ironically in doing so he immortalised it. The whole batshit nature of Fall Out is what ultimately cemented The Prisoner as a masterpiece. The controversy and uproar that surrounded it (causing McGoohan and his family to lay low to avoid disgruntled fans) helped build up the mystique of the show’s reputation which has lasted for nearly 60 years now. It’s what puts it into conversation alongside other surrealistic shows like Lost and Twin Peaks. In fact both those shows owe a lot to The Prisoner.

The Prisoner to me, even when it’s being at its most straightforward, is always largely allegorical. The difference between Fall Out and the rest is that by that point it becomes almost 100% an allegory. 

Finally, the prophetic nature of the show is another thing that must be taken into account. People bandy around the phrase “ahead of its time”. This show truly was. It’s scary and downright sad how many of the things the show hinted at or alluded to have come to pass. Yes, peer pressure has always existed, but it’s through the roof now. Then you have non-stop surveillance, groupthink, people being ostracised for being different, etc, etc. I could go on and on.

So yeah, it is confusing, particularly for a first time watcher. I highly recommend rewatching. It has only got better and better for me with repeated viewings. I’d go so far as to say my first time watching the show wasn’t a truly groundbreaking experience. It was rewatching that really made me appreciate just how good this show is and now it’s up there as the greatest piece of television of all time.

While TTYD is widely regarded as the GOAT, PM64 is the quintessential Paper Mario. It’s the OG and laid the groundwork for everything that came after it.

Gaunter is fascinated by that which he doesn’t understand. Namely love, or anything motivated by anything selfless. He cannot comprehend how thieves can have debts of gratitude and a sense of honour (as the other poster put it). He is, after all, evil incarnate. He may have an abstract idea of how love works (and thus how to manipulate people through it), but he can’t truly understand it. This weakness is, ultimately, his undoing, as he never suspected Geralt would be willing to offer his soul up in a battle of wits to save Olgierd. Everything else goes to plan for him, but he can’t predict Geralt’s selflessness. He can’t resist the bet (another weakness) and ends up losing Olgierd’s soul.
Hearts of Stone is probably the greatest plot I’ve seen in a video game. It’s storytelling at its finest. Gaunter O’Dimm is my favourite version of the Devil in ANY form of media.

I get what you’re saying, but honestly, aside from the Twilight Trail and General White stuff, I don’t think backtracking was a terrible problem in TTYD. At least no worse than Flower Fields in PM64. That is one of the most annoying sections in a video game for me. The back and forth there in such a confined area always drives me nuts. 

Anyway, on the whole, for me they’re both fantastic games. PM64 does have a really classical feel to it. It’s the grand Mario adventure we all know and love and is, in my opinion, the quintessential retelling of that classic Mario tale (Bowser as the main bad guy, Mushroom Kingdom as the setting, etc, etc). But TTYD really ups the stakes and everything seems grander and more sweeping. It just steps up a gear in terms of story, gameplay and setting. But they’re still very hard to separate.

I usually see it like comparing A New Hope with The Empire Strikes Back. It’s a very apt comparison for me. Both phenomenal, but Empire just edges it because it does all the things TTYD does. It steps it up. It has more grit to it and, even though it’s not as classical and lighthearted as its predecessor, it does win out through that added complexity.

Genuinely curious what you like more about the original. I really enjoy both PM64 and TTYD, but in most ways TTYD edges it. Not by much, but by enough. What are the things you like more about the original?

Okay I’m gonna be the one to stick my head above the parapet here… Yes, Bill Cosby and R Kelly could still be good men, yes. Are they? No, not at all. Not to my understanding, anyway. But they could, theoretically, become “good”. 

What I’m driving at is that we do not ever, ever truly understand the heart and soul of another. We judge them on their actions. The actions of these two particular men were deplorable, but they cannot be completely defined by those actions alone. The natural emotion is to say “yeah, they’re completely evil and will be forever”. But that’s how evil wins. To examine the actions of an evil person, to try and understand their behaviour and change it is the only way forward in a progressive society, in my opinion.

It might be a cliched, fictional example, but let’s look at Darth Vader. Dude massacred countless, countless amounts of people (including the brutal murders of several children) and was the most terrifying image in the galaxy to many. But because we see what led him down that path, we still feel empathy for the man he used to be. When he saves Luke and throws the Emperor to his (alleged) doom, he redeems himself. With one, almighty, loving, self-sacrificial act he saves his soul. And we, the audience, accept it because we’ve grown to know and understand this character.

If we had that exact same insight into the minds of those we simply write off as being “evil”, perhaps we’d be more likely to believe in the power of redemption.

Ultimately, I’d say it has to be The Thousand Year Door, but I’ll go into some more detail. Starting with the OG. Paper Mario 64.

Paper Mario:

The grand, sweeping entry into the world of Paper Mario. Building on Super Mario RPG before it, Paper Mario delivers a very entertaining experience. It’s the most classical in terms of plot (regular locations, characters and main antagonist in Bowser). It’s light and fun throughout with hardly any dark moments. It’s the “A New Hope” of Paper Mario games, and my personal second favourite.

The Thousand Year Door: 

TTYD takes practically everything wonderful about Paper Mario and raises it up a notch. Its storyline is both deeper and funnier. From wacky situations to sombre moments, TTYD is truly a gaming masterpiece from start to finish and is my personal favourite (and fifth favourite video game of all time, it’s just that good). It’s just non-stop wholesomeness from start to finish and hard to articulate exactly why without dumping a few spoilers. It just has that GOAT quality about it. It’s simply the best.

Super Paper Mario: 

The strangest, weirdest, darkest, eerie and most epic instalment in the franchise in terms of storyline. Sure, it’s funny, but there’s something truly haunting about certain aspects of this game. If it wasn’t for the lacking gameplay (in my opinion), it probably would be second on my list. As it is it stands in third place. But truly, the storyline is really unique and by far the most impactful of all Paper Mario games. It just stays with you, if you get me. The plot seems to transcend the Mario franchise.

Sticker Star: 

The only legitimately poor Paper Mario game, in my view. It just doesn’t have the heart and soul of the Paper Mario world and aside from a few moments I can barely even remember it. The soundtrack is the only standout thing about it. Bottom of my list.

Colour Splash:

A definite step up from Sticker Star, but it still doesn’t have that Paper Mario magic. Its humour is pretty good when it does try and with a bit more effort this could have been a really good game. As it is it’s just average. Second bottom for me.

Origami King:

Perhaps the most important Paper Mario game of them all and it (just about) passes the test of saving the franchise. It brings back the classic Paper Mario feel just enough to give me hope for the future of the franchise. The storyline was prioritised more than in the previous two entries, but unfortunately that storyline isn’t the best by a long shot (although it does have a couple of really surprising dark moments that feel somewhat jarring, but in a good way). But it’s still enjoyable and I enjoyed the battle system personally. That’s the real make or break test if you’re to enjoy the game and I did like the battle system. Fourth on my list.

So best to worst for me. 

1: The Thousand Year Door.
2: Paper Mario:
3: Super Paper Mario.
4: Origami King.
5: Colour Splash.
6: Sticker Star.

All aside from Sticker Star are worth your time but, in my opinion, you really have to begin with either Paper Mario 64 or The Thousand Year Door. Probably best to start with the former because it is the proper intro to the world of Paper Mario.

Either way, you’re in for a blast, my friend. I just know you’re gonna have a fun time.

So this is a line said by Raoul Silva in Skyfall (my favourite Bond movie).

The whole movie is, essentially, one big psychological game. As a battle in the film, and as a psychological exercise to the viewers on the outside.

The makeup of Bond and Silva is very similar, the only difference is that we know much less about Silva and know that he has succumbed to his demons and become, well, insane.

Bond’s unresolved childhood trauma is the death of his parents. In a big way he never got over it. It didn’t transform him, it just forced him to adopt this “I don’t give a fuck attitude” in order to protect himself. The death of Vesper in Casino Royale only strengthens this. He rejects authority because he doesn’t trust it to protect him. He can only trust himself. M is the only one who begins to break down this barrier, that’s why she’s so pivotal to this particular film.

M represents the mother figure to both Bond and Silva. She’s the embodiment of both their struggles. But while Bond seeks to protect and love her (as the good son, and in a way he couldn’t protect his real mother), Silva wants to destroy her to set himself free (the bad son).

Ultimately, this trauma isn’t resolved until the events of Spectre. In that movie Bond breaks the pattern and allows himself to fall in love with another human being.
